lesson.title: How Children Build a Language From Almost Nothing
lesson.summary: Language acquisition is the process by which children rapidly and largely automatically develop the ability to understand and produce language, combining biological readiness with the language environment around them.
lesson.body:
Language acquisition is the process by which children learn to understand and produce language, and it is one of the most striking achievements of human development. Within a few years, and without formal instruction, typically developing children move from producing no words at all to using a large vocabulary arranged according to a complex grammatical system, one they were never explicitly taught as a set of rules. This fits within the broader themes of developmental psychology: language development shows the same interplay of nature and nurture, the same rough universal sequence with individual variation in timing, and the same sensitive windows that show up in physical and cognitive development more generally.

Historically, the field has been shaped by a genuine debate about how much of language is built in versus learned from the environment. Linguist Noam Chomsky argued that the human brain comes equipped with an innate capacity for language, since children acquire complex grammar far faster and more reliably than general learning principles alone seem able to explain, and children across very different languages and cultures pass through broadly similar developmental milestones. Others emphasize the essential role of the environment: children need to be exposed to language, ideally through rich, responsive interaction with caregivers, and the specific language or languages they hear is the one they learn. The current mainstream view in psychology treats this less as an either-or contest and more as an interaction: children likely bring some biological predispositions that make language learning easier than it would otherwise be, but that capacity still requires real linguistic input and social interaction to develop typically.

Language acquisition follows a broadly predictable sequence, even though the exact timing varies from child to child. Infants first become sensitive to the sounds of language, then move through babbling, then first words, then short combinations of words, and then increasingly complex grammar, a sequence covered in more depth in the chapter on babbling and early speech. Along the way, children show patterns that are strong evidence they are extracting rules rather than only imitating what they hear, such as over-regularizing irregular verbs, saying things like goed instead of went, a mistake no adult around them would model, but one that makes perfect sense if the child has correctly learned the regular past-tense rule and is temporarily over-applying it. Later concepts, including the critical period for language and linguistic relativity, build directly on this basic acquisition process, asking respectively whether there is a biological window in which language learning works best, and whether the particular language a person acquires can shape how they think.
